place.posBasis: rough estimate of the approach road

actions: driving from Honolulu in his 1930 Plymouth, he is strafed by a Zero about a mile short of the field
jumps out and takes cover in a ditch, then drives on
reaches the field about 08:05 and takes charge; later hit by fragments, he stays in command
vignettes.outcome: Wounded but remained on duty.
vignettes.source: Cressman & Wenger, Infamous Day; Warfare History Network, 'Embattled Marines at Air Station Ewa'
vignettes.note: Arrival time 08:05 is from the USMC monograph as I recall it.

place.detail: A parked SBD-2 dive bomber on the Ewa flight line
place.posBasis: airfield reference coordinates

who.name: William G. Turner
who.role: Stood on the wing feeding the ammunition belt; mortally wounded

actions: between attacks the two climb onto a parked dive bomber
Peters swings the flexible .30-calibre gun in the rear cockpit while Turner stands on the wing holding the belt
they fire at the dive bombers and fighters of the later attacks
two Zeros concentrate on the plane and hit both men
vignettes.outcome: Both wounded; Turner died several days later at Ewa Plantation Hospital.
vignettes.source: Cressman & Wenger, Infamous Day; American Rifleman, 'Remember Pearl Harbor: The Men and the Guns'
vignettes.note: Ewa was attacked three times; the start time here is approximate.

place.detail: Tent area, the short runway and the P-40s of the 44th Pursuit Squadron parked beside it; the beach beyond
place.posBasis: estimate of the 1941 strip

who.name: George A. Whiteman
who.role: Shot down as his P-40 left the ground; killed

who.name: Samuel W. Bishop
who.role: Got airborne, was shot down into the sea and swam ashore wounded

who.name: Raymond F. McBriarty
who.role: Fired the rear gun of a parked O-47

vignettes.countNote: about a dozen P-40s on the field for gunnery training, their guns removed for cleaning
actions: about 08:30 a single fighter strafes the tent area
crews rush to re-install guns and load the P-40s
about 09:00 nine Zeros strafe the field as the pilots try to take off
Christiansen is hit getting in; Whiteman is shot down just after lifting off and crashes in flames by the beach; Bishop goes into the sea offshore and swims back
soldiers fire rifles, BARs and a machine gun in the rear cockpit of a parked O-47
vignettes.dress: Khaki, fatigues; pilots without flying gear
vignettes.outcome: Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, is named for him.
vignettes.medal: Silver Star (Whiteman and Christiansen posthumous; Bishop; McBriarty)
vignettes.source: Arakaki & Kuborn, ch. VI; Kadena AB, 'Three 44th Pursuit Squadron pilots among heroes at Pearl Harbor'; Hawaii Aviation, 'December 7, 1941'
vignettes.note: A B-17C (Lt Richards) also crash-landed here and was strafed. Bellows deaths appear as 2 (the pilots) or 5 in an early Air Force table. McBriarty and the Silver Stars are from memory of the Air Force history.

place.detail: In the air west and south-west of Oahu, approaching Barbers Point and Ewa
place.posBasis: rough estimate of the approach off Barbers Point

who.name: Clarence E. Dickinson
who.role: Shot down near Ewa; parachuted and hitch-hiked to Pearl Harbor

vignettes.countNote: 18 two-seat SBDs sent ahead from Enterprise
actions: Enterprise's scouts, launched at 06:18 to land at Ford Island, fly into the first wave
Gonzalez is heard on the radio pleading with someone not to shoot, then telling his gunner to stand by to launch the rubber boat
several SBDs are shot down by Zeros or by American anti-aircraft fire; survivors land at Ewa and Ford Island under fire from both sides
vignettes.outcome: Gonzalez and Kozelek were never found. Enterprise lost several SBDs that morning and three Wildcats to friendly fire that night.
vignettes.quote: Please don't shoot! This is six-baker-three, an American plane!
vignettes.source: Scouting Squadron Six action report (NHHC); Warfare History Network; Lord, Day of Infamy
vignettes.note: Wording of the transmission varies between accounts; time approximate. SBD losses are given as 6 or 7 aircraft.

place.detail: Orbiting at about 3,000 m over Pearl Harbor and southern Oahu
place.posBasis: centre of the harbor; his track is not recorded

actions: leads the high-level bombers down Battleship Row; cloud and smoke force a second run
anti-aircraft fire holes the fuselage and nearly cuts a control cable
after bombing he circles the harbor with binoculars, noting hits and watching the second wave
stays over Oahu to gather stragglers and is among the last aircraft back aboard Akagi, about 13:00
vignettes.dress: Brown flight suit, life vest, helmet with hachimaki
vignettes.outcome: His damage report shaped Nagumo's assessment. The claim that he pressed for a third strike is disputed.
vignettes.source: Fuchida (Proceedings 1952); Prange, At Dawn We Slept; Zimm, Attack on Pearl Harbor
vignettes.note: Largely Fuchida's own account. The time of his return and the third-strike argument are contested by Zimm and by Parshall.

place.detail: Ammunition tunnels in Aliamanu Crater, and the roads from Fort Shafter, Fort Kamehameha, Schofield and Camp Malakole to the batteries' field positions
place.posBasis: rough estimate of the crater

who.name: Gun crews of the 64th, 97th, 98th and 251st Coast Artillery (AA)

vignettes.countNote: 31 anti-aircraft batteries on Oahu
actions: under Alert No. 1 the mobile batteries are parked in gun parks with their ammunition in the crater depot
at the alarm the crews hitch up and drive to their field positions while trucks queue at the crater for 3-inch rounds
the fixed battery on Sand Island is firing by about 08:15
elsewhere soldiers fire rifles, BARs and machine guns from the gun parks
vignettes.outcome: Only about four of the 31 batteries were in action before the attack ended.
vignettes.source: Conn, Engelman & Fairchild, Guarding the United States and Its Outposts, ch. VII; Joint Congressional Committee report
vignettes.note: The Sand Island time and the four-of-31 figure are from memory of the Army history. Burgin's name unverified.

place.detail: Ordnance machine shop area, Fort Kamehameha, between Hickam and the harbor entrance
place.posBasis: rough estimate

vignettes.countNote: plus soldiers sheltering near the building
actions: a Zero hit while strafing Hickam flies low across Fort Kamehameha
it clips palm trees and smashes against the ordnance shop where soldiers have taken cover
vignettes.outcome: Pilot killed; several soldiers on the ground were killed or injured. The wreck was the first Zero examined by US intelligence.
vignettes.source: Lansdale, 'The Lost Pearl Harbor Attack Aircraft' (j-aircraft.com); Wenger, Cressman & Di Virgilio
vignettes.note: Written from memory; time, building and casualty count are unverified. Do not render specifics without checking.

place.detail: KGMB radio studio, Kapiolani Boulevard, Honolulu
place.posBasis: rough estimate of the 1941 studio

vignettes.countNote: studio staff; approximate
actions: shortly after 08:00 the Sunday music is interrupted: all Army, Navy and Marine personnel are to report for duty
the call is repeated at 08:15 and 08:30; police, firemen and doctors are called in too
about 08:40 Edwards comes on himself to convince doubters that it is not a drill
the station keeps broadcasting orders and warnings until the Army takes the stations off the air late in the morning
vignettes.outcome: Most of Honolulu learned of the attack from these broadcasts.
vignettes.quote: This is no maneuver. This is the real McCoy!
vignettes.source: Lord, Day of Infamy; Wikipedia, 'Webley Edwards'; Honolulu Star-Advertiser
vignettes.note: Times 08:04, 08:15, 08:30 and 08:40 are Lord's as I recall them. Another chronology gives 08:08 and 08:15 for the recalls and about 09:00 for Edwards. Wording varies ('This is not a maneuver'; 'no exercise').

place.detail: Scattered across the city: Nuuanu and Kukui Streets, Judd Street, McCully, the Washington Place and Iolani Palace area, Iwilei, Liliha, Dowsett, Diamond Head
place.posBasis: Nuuanu Avenue at Kukui Street (estimate); see 'sites'

who.name: Joseph K. Adams, John K. Adams, Joseph McCabe Sr., David Kahookele
who.rank: civilians, Pearl Harbor Navy Yard workers
who.role: Killed when a shell burst beside their car on Judd Street while driving to work

vignettes.countNote: about 40 separate explosions in the city (one newspaper count gives 51 sites on Oahu)
actions: Navy 5-inch anti-aircraft shells fired without fuzes set, or with faulty ones, arc over the city and burst on impact
one bursts beside a car of yard workers on Judd Street, riddling it
another hits a small restaurant and shops at Nuuanu and Kukui, killing about a dozen people including a family and several young amateur boxers
one bursts near the governor's residence, killing a passer-by
people run into the streets to look, then for cover; police and ambulances thread through traffic heading to Pearl Harbor
vignettes.dress: Sunday civilian dress: aloha shirts, dresses, church clothes, kimono among older Japanese residents
vignettes.outcome: Nearly all the damage in Honolulu and most civilian deaths came from American anti-aircraft shells, not Japanese bombs. Property damage was put at about half a million dollars.
vignettes.source: NPS, 'Civilian Casualties'; MilitaryHistoryNow, 'The Forgotten Casualties of Pearl Harbor'; Honolulu Star-Advertiser; Lord, Day of Infamy

sites.name: Nuuanu Avenue and Kukui Street
sites.note: about 12 killed (count and victims' identities from memory)

sites.name: Judd Street
sites.note: car of Navy Yard workers; 3 or 4 killed

vignettes.note: The count of explosions (40 or 51), the Nuuanu-Kukui toll and the Judd Street toll (a Navy photo caption says three killed in the car) are not settled in the sources I could check. The four names given for Judd Street are from memory of the NPS civilian list and must be checked against it before display. All site coordinates are street-corner estimates.

place.detail: King Street at McCully Street: a block of wooden shops and houses, largely Japanese-owned
place.posBasis: street-corner estimate

who.name: Honolulu Fire Department companies not sent to Hickam

vignettes.countNote: dozens made homeless
actions: shells burst at the corner and a drugstore and neighbouring shops catch fire
the fire runs through the wooden block; residents carry out children, bedding and shop stock
neighbours form bucket lines with garden hoses until engines arrive
the injured are carried to the first-aid station at Lunalilo School
vignettes.outcome: The worst single area of damage in the city; several residents died.
vignettes.source: Honolulu Star-Advertiser; Densho Encyclopedia, 'December 7, 1941'; Lord, Day of Infamy

place.posBasis: estimate of the school site

who.name: Daniel K. Inouye
who.role: McKinley High School senior and Red Cross first-aid instructor; later US Senator

vignettes.countNote: aid-station volunteers and casualties

the aid station phones for him and he cycles there through streets full of people
he helps carry and treat casualties from the McCully shell bursts and fire
the school building itself is hit and its roof burns; a neighbouring building burns with people trapped inside
vignettes.dress: Civilian; he had been putting on church clothes

place.detail: Churches in downtown Honolulu and base chapels; an outdoor altar being set up at Hickam
place.posBasis: Iolani Palace as a downtown reference point

actions: families walk and drive to early services in Sunday clothes
people stand in the streets and on roofs watching the smoke, most taking it for manoeuvres
servicemen in the pews leave when the radio recall spreads; services break up
vignettes.dress: Sunday best; servicemen on liberty in whites or khaki
vignettes.source: Lord, Day of Infamy; Inouye memoir; general accounts
vignettes.note: Generic colour. No individual congregation scene was verified; do not attach names or places.

who.name: Mary Ann Ramsey
who.role: Daughter of Lt Cdr Logan Ramsey

who.name: Navy wives and children of Ford Island

vignettes.countNote: the families of the senior officers' row; dozens
actions: fathers run for their stations as the first bombs fall
mothers and children hurry along the row to the old gun emplacement under Quarters K, known as the dungeon
oil-covered, burned sailors who have swum ashore from Battleship Row are brought in; the girls give them water, cigarettes and blankets
the bachelor officers' quarters becomes a receiving hospital
vignettes.outcome: No Ford Island dependants were killed.

place.detail: Homes and shops in Honolulu, Pearl City, Ewa and Wahiawa
place.posBasis: central Honolulu reference

who.name: Civilian children
who.role: Killed by shell bursts and strafing

vignettes.countNote: the NPS list of 49 civilian dead includes about a dozen children, the youngest three months old
actions: children are playing outside or eating breakfast when shells burst in residential streets
parents carry injured children to aid stations and hospitals
vignettes.source: NPS, 'Civilian Casualties' (names and ages); Smithsonian, 'The Children of Pearl Harbor'

place.detail: Tripler General Hospital (the old wooden hospital by Fort Shafter), and the lecture hall in Honolulu where the city's doctors had gathered
place.posBasis: rough estimate of the 1941 hospital

who.name: Army Nurse Corps nurses
who.role: 82 Army nurses were serving on Oahu at Tripler, Schofield and Hickam

vignettes.countNote: hundreds of casualties
actions: Honolulu doctors are assembling for Moorhead's Sunday lecture when a call comes for surgeons at Tripler at once
they drive to the hospital and operate in teams for the rest of the day
trucks and ambulances unload wounded from Hickam on the lawns; nurses sort them and give morphine
civilian volunteers queue to give blood
vignettes.dress: White nurses' uniforms; surgeons in civilian clothes then gowns
vignettes.outcome: Tripler was overwhelmed with burn and shock cases.
vignettes.source: health.mil, 'Tripler Hospital on Pearl Harbor Day and the Nurses Who Answered the Call'; Army Medical Department histories; Lord, Day of Infamy
vignettes.note: The lecture story and the figure of 82 nurses are from memory; time approximate.

place.detail: University of Hawaii campus in Manoa, St Louis Heights, and the beach positions of the 298th and 299th Infantry
place.posBasis: University of Hawaii campus (estimate)

who.name: Nisei soldiers of the 298th and 299th Infantry (Hawaii National Guard)

vignettes.countNote: several hundred cadets
actions: Japanese American guardsmen go to their beach positions with their regiments
ROTC cadets answer a radio call, draw Springfield rifles and a few rounds and are sent to St Louis Heights against rumoured paratroopers
that afternoon they are sworn into the Hawaii Territorial Guard and posted at power stations, reservoirs and Iolani Palace
Japanese American residents queue to give blood and volunteer at aid stations

place.detail: Japanese consulate on Nuuanu Avenue; homes across Honolulu; the Immigration Station on Ala Moana
place.posBasis: estimate of the consulate

who.name: Robert L. Shivers
who.rank: FBI Special Agent in Charge, Honolulu
who.role: Directed the pick-ups from the custodial detention list

who.name: Japanese community leaders
who.role: Priests, language-school teachers, consular agents, businessmen

vignettes.countNote: several hundred detained within days
actions: police arrive at the consulate and find staff burning papers in a tub
FBI agents, Army intelligence officers and police go house to house with a prepared list; men are taken from their homes, often with a few minutes to dress
detainees are held at the Immigration Station and then on Sand Island

place.detail: Governor's office in Iolani Palace
place.posBasis: Iolani Palace

actions: late in the morning the governor proclaims a defence emergency over the radio; a shell has burst near Washington Place, his residence, earlier in the morning
the Army orders the radio stations off the air so that they cannot guide aircraft
Short calls on the governor after noon and presses for martial law
the governor signs the proclamation about 15:30 after telephoning the President; it is announced later in the afternoon
vignettes.outcome: Hawaii remained under martial law until October 1944.
vignettes.source: Densho Encyclopedia, 'Joseph Poindexter'; Conn, Engelman & Fairchild, ch. VIII; Honolulu Star-Bulletin archives

place.detail: A field near Puuwai village on Niihau, about 240 km west-north-west of Pearl Harbor
place.posBasis: rough estimate of Puuwai

who.name: Hawila Kaleohano
who.role: Disarmed the pilot and took his papers

who.name: Yoshio Harada
who.role: Helped the pilot, then shot himself

vignettes.countNote: plus the villagers
actions: a damaged Zero crash-lands near the village in the early afternoon
Kaleohano pulls the pilot out and takes his pistol and papers; the villagers, with no radio, treat him as a guest
over the week the pilot wins over a resident of Japanese descent, takes hostages and burns his aircraft
on 13 December Ben Kanahele, shot three times, picks the pilot up and dashes him against a wall; his wife strikes him with a rock
vignettes.dress: Japanese flight suit; villagers in work clothes
vignettes.outcome: Pilot killed; Harada dead by suicide. The episode was later cited in arguments for removing Japanese Americans on the mainland.
vignettes.medal: Medal for Merit and Purple Heart (Ben Kanahele)
vignettes.source: Wikipedia, 'Niihau incident'; Smithsonian Air & Space, 'The Niihau Zero'
vignettes.note: Outside the main animation area. Landing time is approximate; the pilot's rank is given variously.

place.detail: Waimanalo beach in front of Bellows Field; the midget submarine HA-19 is aground on the reef offshore
place.posBasis: rough estimate of the beach

actions: with a broken gyrocompass HA-19 has spent 7 December striking reefs off the harbor entrance and drifting east
she grounds off Bellows before dawn; the scuttling charge fails and both men swim for shore through surf
Inagaki drowns; Sakamaki collapses on the sand
Akui, on patrol with Plybon, sees a figure at the water's edge and takes him at gunpoint
vignettes.dress: Sakamaki came ashore nearly naked; the guardsmen wore Army khaki with helmets and rifles
vignettes.outcome: Sakamaki became US prisoner of war No. 1. HA-19 was hauled ashore, studied and toured the United States selling war bonds.
vignettes.source: Hawaii Department of Defense, '1941 capture of the first Japanese POW of World War II'; Wikipedia, 'Kazuo Sakamaki' and 'David Akui'; af.mil, 'Pearl Harbor mini-sub mission fails, first prisoner captured'
vignettes.note: Clock time is my estimate for 'predawn' (sunrise was about 06:27 by 1941 Hawaii time). One account says two Japanese American MPs made the pick-up. Akui's rank is given as corporal or sergeant.

place.detail: On the upturned bottom of Oklahoma, beside Maryland; air compressors on a barge alongside, floodlights at night
place.posBasis: Oklahoma berth estimate

who.name: Julio DeCastro
who.rank: civilian, Leadingman Caulker and Chipper, Shop 11, Pearl Harbor Navy Yard

who.name: E. P. Kranzfelder
who.role: Brought the ship's plans to guide the cutting

who.name: Stephen Bower Young
who.role: One of eleven men freed from a single compartment after about 25 hours

vignettes.countNote: about 20 yard workers with sailors from Oklahoma, Maryland and other ships
actions: sailors on the hull hear tapping within minutes of the capsizing and tap back
a first cut with a torch on 7 December fills a void with fumes and two trapped men suffocate; the crews switch to pneumatic chipping hammers
working from plans, they chip rectangular holes through the bottom plating and through inner bulkheads, plugging the cuts as air escapes and water rises inside
men are pulled out soaked in oil, some after more than a day in the dark; sailors on Maryland cheer each one
the first group comes out about 08:00 on 8 December and others through that day
vignettes.dress: Yard workers in work clothes; rescued men in oil-soaked skivvies
vignettes.outcome: 32 men were saved. DeCastro received a commendation from the Commandant, 14th Naval District.
vignettes.source: Smithsonian, 'The Civilian Worker Who Spearheaded Pearl Harbor's Most Successful Rescue Mission'; Warfare History Network, 'The USS Oklahoma Rescue Mission'; Wallin, ch. XI; NAVSEA
vignettes.note: The 32 total and DeCastro's role are firm. The hour of the last rescue is not: I have entered 02:30 on 9 December from memory, but one search summary gave 09:00 on 9 December and others imply the work ended on 8 December. Start time on the 7th is approximate.

place.detail: A sealed, dry storeroom forward and deep in the sunken West Virginia
place.posBasis: West Virginia berth estimate

actions: three men are sealed in an airtight compartment when the ship sinks
Marine sentries on the quays hear banging from inside the hull at night for more than two weeks
no cut can be made: a torch risks explosion and opening the space would flood it
vignettes.outcome: When the ship was raised in 1942 salvors found the three bodies, with a calendar on which sixteen days, 7 to 23 December, had been crossed off.
vignettes.source: Honolulu Advertiser (1995) and later press accounts drawing on salvage officers and families; Wallin, ch. XII
vignettes.note: Widely reported but not in the official action report; the search did not return it. For narration only.

complements.note: Figures are men assigned to the ship on 7 December unless stated. Navy data given to the Roberts Commission put at least 90 percent of officers and men aboard their ships when the attack began, so 'aboard' is roughly 0.9 to 0.95 of 'assigned'. Only the Arizona figure is an official published count; the rest are approximations from standard references and should be shown as 'about'.

arizona.note: NPS figures. The 335 survivors include men who were ashore; some sources give 334 or 337.

california.note: Battle Force flagship, so the figure includes flag staff; approximate. Dead 98 to 105 by source.

nevada.note: Complement approximate. Dead 50 (NPS table) to 60 (common figure).

pennsylvania.note: Fleet flagship, in Drydock No. 1. Complement approximate. Dead 15 plus 14 missing in the action report; 18 in the NPS table.

hawaiian_department_army.note: Army strength on Oahu, from memory of the Army history.

ships_in_harbor.note: NHHC says some 86 Pacific Fleet ships excluding small craft; other counts run 96 to 101; NPS says about 150 including yard and service craft. No aircraft carriers were present.

liberty.text: At least 90 percent of officers and enlisted men were aboard their ships when the attack came (Navy data submitted to the Roberts Commission, reproduced in the congressional hearings).
About 11,000 soldiers and sailors had been on pass in Honolulu on the night of 6 December, roughly ten percent of the force (Wallin).

Overnight liberty for enlisted men generally expired before morning colours; married officers and senior petty officers with families ashore were the main absentees. The captains of Nevada, Oklahoma, California and Tennessee were ashore; those of Arizona, West Virginia and Pennsylvania were aboard.
A per-class breakdown often quoted (battleship enlisted about 95 percent aboard, officers 60 to 70 percent) could not be verified in this research.

routine.text: Sunday 'holiday routine' in port: late reveille, no drills, working parties limited to essentials. Many men who had been ashore on Saturday night were still in their bunks.
Breakfast on the mess decks, roughly 07:00 to 07:30; mess cooks clearing up afterwards. Officers at breakfast in wardrooms.
The forenoon watch relieves; officers of the deck in whites on quarterdecks with a quartermaster, bugler and messenger.
First call to colours: the blue Prep flag goes up on the Navy Yard signal tower. Colour details, bands and Marine guards stand by aft; a jack party at the bow.
Morning colours: ensign and jack hoisted, anthem or bugle call. Church services were to follow on fantails under awnings; church and liberty boats were already crossing the harbor.

Ships lay in a relaxed watertight condition, with doors and hatches open for ventilation; California had manhole covers off double-bottom voids for an inspection. Battleships had one boiler lit for auxiliary power and needed about two hours to raise steam.

Fleet readiness order: on each battleship two machine guns manned with ammunition and crews told off for two 5-inch anti-aircraft guns; ready-ammunition boxes at the guns, on some ships padlocked with keys held by the duty officer.

Army on Alert No. 1 (sabotage): aircraft parked wingtip to wingtip in the open under guard, ammunition boxed in storerooms and at Aliamanu Crater, mobile anti-aircraft batteries in their gun parks. Radar stations had operated 04:00 to 07:00 only.
On the airfields: men at breakfast, asleep in barracks and tents, or on guard. Hickam expected twelve B-17s from California at about 08:00.
Honolulu: a quiet Sunday morning, people at breakfast or on their way to church; KGMB had played music through the night for the incoming B-17s.
Weather: partly cloudy with cloud on the mountains, light north-east trade wind, good visibility over the harbor. Sunrise had been at about 06:26 by 1941 Hawaii time.

dress.group: Navy enlisted on watch, colour details, bands, boat crews, liberty and church parties
dress.dress: Undress whites: white jumper, white trousers, white hat, black shoes.
Skivvies: white T-shirt or undershirt and shorts; many barefoot or in pyjamas. This is what a large share of the men on the battleships were wearing when they ran to their guns.

dress.group: Navy working parties, engineers, yard craft crews
dress.dress: Dungarees: blue chambray shirt and denim trousers, white hat.
Service dress whites (high collar) for watch officers and those going ashore; khaki for aviators and many working officers; several came on deck in pyjamas.
Khaki shirt and trousers with field hat or garrison cap; dungarees for aircraft mechanics.
Khaki cotton shirt and trousers; blue denim fatigues for details; mechanics' coveralls; old-pattern flat steel helmets once issued; Springfield rifles and BARs.
Whatever they woke in: Welch and Taylor in tuxedo trousers, Rasmussen in purple pyjamas.
White ward uniforms and caps; corpsmen in whites.
Aloha shirts, cotton dresses, Sunday church clothes; yard workers in work clothes; Honolulu firemen in dark uniforms and leather helmets.
Brown one-piece flight suits, kapok life vests, fur-lined leather helmets and goggles, many with hachimaki headbands.
White or khaki working uniforms and soft caps.
Navy medical reports stressed that flash burns were worst on bare skin: men in shorts and undershirts were burned far more severely than men in long sleeves and trousers.

response.text: Manned ready machine guns on the ships opened fire almost at once. NHHC states that about a quarter of the fleet's .50-calibre anti-aircraft machine guns were manned and reacted almost immediately.
Within about five minutes most battleship anti-aircraft batteries were firing; cruisers averaged about four minutes and destroyers about seven for their full batteries.
response.source: As I recall the Joint Congressional Committee report; the search could not confirm the figures verbatim

response.text: The 'locked ammunition' stories are true mainly of ships under repair or overhaul. Mine Division One borrowed .50-calibre ammunition from a neighbouring ship and opened fire within 15 minutes; Downes's machine guns were firing within 15 minutes. On some ships ready-box padlocks were knocked off with hammers and axes.
Where power failed (California, West Virginia, New Orleans) ammunition was passed by hand up ladders.
response.source: Action reports; Medal of Honor citations

response.text: The Japanese reported American fire becoming intense within about five minutes of the first bomb.
response.source: Nagumo's report as summarised in secondary sources

response.text: Army anti-aircraft: the fixed 3-inch battery on Sand Island was firing by about 08:15; only about four of 31 batteries were in action before the raid ended, because guns and ammunition had to be moved to field positions. Wheeler had no anti-aircraft guns, trenches or shelters.
On the airfields men fought back with rifles, pistols, BARs and machine guns stripped from aircraft, typically within 10 to 20 minutes, after breaking into locked supply rooms.

Destroyer Helm, already under way, cleared the entrance and fired on a midget submarine on the reef at 08:17; Monaghan got under way at 08:27; Nevada at 08:40; cruiser St. Louis cleared the channel about 10:04.

A lull of roughly 08:25 to 08:50 separated the waves; it was used to bring up ammunition and site guns. The second wave met far heavier fire: 20 of the 29 Japanese aircraft lost fell in the second wave.
About a dozen Army fighters got into the air from Haleiwa, Wheeler and Bellows between 08:30 and 09:30.
The last attacks ended about 09:45; the last Japanese aircraft left the Oahu area about 10:00.

total.note: The standard official total. The National Park Service uses 2,390 for its name-by-name count.

civilian.note: 68 killed and 35 wounded are the long-standing official figures. The NPS list names 49 civilian dead; other counts give 48, 54 or 57 killed and up to about 280 injured. Most died in Honolulu from American anti-aircraft shells.

japanese.note: The often-quoted 129 Japanese dead adds the crew of submarine I-70, sunk on 10 December. Aircraft: 9 in the first wave, 20 in the second.

arizona.note: Navy and Marines; 73 of the dead were Marines (from memory).

oklahoma.note: DANFS: 20 officers and 395 men killed or missing at the time, 32 wounded.

west_virginia.note: One survivor-report summary says 2 officers and 102 men.

california.note: 98 in early reports, 100 commonly, 104 to 105 in NPS lists.

nevada.note: 50 in the NPS table and NHHC caption; 57 or 60 in other lists.

pennsylvania.note: NPS table; action report 15 killed, 14 missing, 38 wounded.

enterprise_air_group.note: SBD crews lost in the morning plus Wildcat pilots shot down by friendly fire that night; from memory.

hickam_field.note: Figures on the Hickam memorial and 15th Wing fact sheets. An early tally gives 121 killed, 274 wounded and 37 missing; another fact sheet says 139 killed.

wheeler_field.note: Also given as 38 killed and 59 wounded, or 37 killed, 6 missing and 53 wounded.

bellows_field.note: The two pilots; an early Air Force table shows 5 killed and 9 wounded.

army_air_forces_total_early_tally.note: Arakaki & Kuborn's contemporary tally as I recall it; it cannot be reconciled exactly with the later per-field figures or with the Army total of 218.

kaneohe_nas.note: 18 Navy men plus 2 civilians on the NPS list; Navy dead also given as 17 or 19.

ewa_mcas.note: Four Marines named on the NPS list.

honolulu_and_other_civilian_areas.note: My count of Honolulu names on the NPS list from memory; the rest of the 49 were at Hickam, Pearl City, Wahiawa, Waipahu, Ewa, Kaneohe, John Rodgers Airport and Pearl Harbor.

john_rodgers_airport.note: Robert Tyce. Three soldiers in rented light planes were also lost offshore (unverified).

niihau.note: The Japanese pilot and Yoshio Harada, both on 13 December; not part of the 2,403.

medalsOfHonor.name: Mervyn S. Bennion
medalsOfHonor.summary: Mortally wounded on the bridge; refused to be moved and kept directing the ship's defence until he died.

medalsOfHonor.name: John W. Finn
medalsOfHonor.summary: Manned a .50-calibre machine gun on an instruction stand in the open for over two hours though wounded many times.

medalsOfHonor.name: Francis C. Flaherty
medalsOfHonor.summary: Stayed in his turret holding a flashlight so the crew could escape as the ship capsized.

medalsOfHonor.name: Samuel G. Fuqua
medalsOfHonor.summary: Directed firefighting, rescue and the abandonment of the ship from the quarterdeck after the magazine explosion.

medalsOfHonor.name: Edwin J. Hill
medalsOfHonor.summary: Cast off the lines from the quay and swam back aboard; killed on the forecastle trying to let go the anchors.

medalsOfHonor.name: Herbert C. Jones
medalsOfHonor.summary: Organised a party passing ammunition by hand; mortally wounded, he ordered his rescuers to leave him.

medalsOfHonor.name: Isaac C. Kidd
medalsOfHonor.summary: Commander Battleship Division One; went to the signal bridge and was killed when the ship blew up.

medalsOfHonor.name: Jackson C. Pharris
medalsOfHonor.summary: Though injured by the first torpedo, set up a hand-supply ammunition train and repeatedly rescued unconscious shipmates from flooding, oil-filled compartments.

medalsOfHonor.name: Thomas J. Reeves
medalsOfHonor.summary: Passed ammunition by hand in a burning passageway until overcome by smoke and fire.

medalsOfHonor.name: Donald K. Ross
medalsOfHonor.summary: Kept the forward and after dynamo rooms running alone until blinded and unconscious, and returned each time he was revived.

medalsOfHonor.name: Robert R. Scott
medalsOfHonor.summary: Refused to leave his flooding air-compressor station so that the guns would have air.

medalsOfHonor.name: Peter Tomich
medalsOfHonor.summary: Stayed in the boiler rooms securing the boilers and getting his men out as the ship capsized.

medalsOfHonor.name: Franklin Van Valkenburgh
medalsOfHonor.summary: Commanding officer; killed on the bridge when the forward magazines exploded.

medalsOfHonor.name: James R. Ward
medalsOfHonor.summary: Stayed in his turret holding a flashlight so the crew could escape as the ship capsized.

medalsOfHonor.name: Cassin Young
medalsOfHonor.summary: Blown overboard by Arizona's explosion, swam back, countermanded abandon ship, got Vestal under way and beached her.

medalsOfHonorNote: Fifteen Medals of Honor, all Navy, were awarded for Oahu on 7 December 1941; ten were posthumous. A sixteenth for that date went to First Lieutenant George H. Cannon, USMC, at Midway. Other decorations for the attack are commonly listed as 51 Navy Crosses, 53 Silver Stars, 4 Navy and Marine Corps Medals, 1 Distinguished Flying Cross, 4 Distinguished Service Crosses, 1 Distinguished Service Medal and 3 Bronze Stars (figures from memory of the standard list; unverified).
